22.0.0.en: 1 The burden of the valley of vision. What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops? 2 Thou that art full of stirs, a tumultuous city, a joyous city: thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle. 3 All thy rulers are fled together, they are bound by the archers: all that are found in thee are bound together, which have fled from far. 4 Therefore said I, Look away from me; I will weep bitterly, labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people. 5 For it is a day of trouble, and of treading down, and of perplexity by the Lord GOD of hosts in the valley of vision, breaking down the walls, and of crying to the mountains. 6 And Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield. 7 And it shall come to pass, that thy choicest valleys shall be full of chariots, and the horsemen shall set themselves in array at the gate.

22.0.1.en: "The burden of the valley of vision. What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops?" [1].

22.0.2.en: * What is meant by the valley of vision?

22.0.3.en: A. Jewish scholars see that this title is fitting for Jerusalem because it is the city in which God gave His servants visions and revelations. Perhaps the inspired word used this title to awaken in them the insight that had been blotted out. This Jerusalem, whose siege God permitted, is His city in which He set up His temple to reveal Himself, His kingdom and the glories of His heavens in it, so that it might be a secret of blessing to mankind, but the corruption of its people blotted out its insight.

22.0.4.en: B. It is called "the valley of vision" although Jerusalem was not built on a valley but on mountains; yet the presence of high mountains around it makes it, in relation to these mountains, like a valley. In any case, God wanted to make of His city a high, firm mountain, but the corruption of its people brought it down to become a valley.

22.0.5.en: Some ask: what siege is the prophet speaking of here?

22.0.6.en: Is it the siege carried out by Sennacherib, or the siege of Esarhaddon in the days of Manasseh? Or is it the siege of Nebuchadnezzar, or of Titus?!

22.0.7.en: Some see that it is the siege of Sennacherib, although from the spiritual side it applies to every siege in which Jerusalem fell, and more so it applies to the siege that comes upon our inner Jerusalem, the heart, the mind and the soul.

22.0.8.en: * The going up to the housetops [1]: The people did not expect that God, who loves His city and declares His presence especially inside the Holy of Holies, where His glory appeared in the Shekinah (the Ark of the Covenant), would permit the siege of His city by the pagans; therefore they went up to the housetops to see for themselves what had befallen the city from outside.

22.0.9.en: Perhaps their going up to the roof points to their concern for the outside and not the inside, for appearances and not the depths; instead of entering the house of their inner souls to discover the secret of their weakness, they were concerned with what is on the surface. Therefore the prophet rebukes them, saying:

22.1.0.en: "Thou that art full of stirs, a tumultuous city, a joyous city" [2]. These are outward marks, for Jerusalem, imitating the capitals of the surrounding countries, boasted and rejoiced in noisy appearances instead of the hidden, silent return to God, the secret of her pride, her strength and her gladness.

22.1.1.en: * "Thy slain men are not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle. All thy rulers are fled together, they are bound by the archers: all that are found in thee are bound together, which have fled from far. Therefore said I, Look away from me; I will weep bitterly, labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people" [2-4].

22.1.2.en: Isaiah saw what had befallen the city of his God, which was very dear to him, and asked that no one comfort him because of the intensity of the bitterness of his soul. He saw the army of Jerusalem going out into the fields under the command of rulers who did not die by the sword, but fled out of fear, and the enemy overtook them, captured them and humbled them.

22.1.3.en: "Thy slain men are not slain with the sword"... for the people stabbed themselves with the fiery darts of lusts, and isolated themselves from God, the source of their life, and so their souls fell slain before the outward ruin came. The prophet saw what is more dangerous than Sennacherib and his army: surrender to sins and abominations and the practical denial of the faith. For sin "hath cast down many wounded: yea, many strong men have been slain by her. Her house is the way to hell, going down to the chambers of death" (Prov 7:26-27).

22.1.4.en: The prophet had nothing left but to pour himself out in tears before God; this is what every wise spiritual leader does when he sees the people of God go astray or souls perish, and so he says with the prophet Jeremiah: "Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!" (Jer 9:1). The Lord of the prophets Himself "beheld the city, and wept over it" (Lk 19:41).

22.1.5.en: * I do not deny that the first Jerusalem was destroyed because of the evil of its inhabitants, but I ask: is it not fitting for you to weep over your spiritual Jerusalem?!

22.1.6.en: If anyone sins after receiving the mysteries of the truth, he is wept over, because he was of Jerusalem and no longer is...

22.1.7.en: Let our Jerusalem be wept over, because on account of sin the enemies (the evil spirits) surround it with a rampart and besiege it and leave in it not one stone upon another.

22.1.8.en: Origen * He (the Lord) wept over Jerusalem because He wanted blessedness for her - as I said - by her accepting faith in Him and welcoming peace with God. This is what He called them to through Isaiah, saying: "Let us make peace with him" [(Isa 27:5) the Septuagint]... let us make peace with God through faith.

22.1.9.en: St. Cyril the Great * Our Savior does not cease to weep even until now, through His chosen ones, whenever He sees a person leaving the good life and walking in the evil way.

22.1.11.en: The people of Jerusalem, especially the civil and religious leaders, lived in luxury and indulgence, spending their nights in parties, eating and drinking, while Isaiah stood warning and cautioning. Now the people stand on the housetops and see the ruin with their own eyes, while Isaiah's heart is broken with grief and bitterness; he enters his chamber and weeps with abundant tears, that perhaps God would have compassion on His people. He lived bold and frank in his directions, and loving and tender in his feelings.

22.2.0.en: Isaiah describes what befell Jerusalem of trouble, treading down, perplexity and crying [5], for despair came over the whole city; no one knew how to act or where to go. Perhaps some called for strengthening the walls, others called for fleeing to the mountains, and another group preferred to surrender. Jerusalem was transformed from the valley of divine vision, the giver of peace, into a valley that confuses and shatters the soul... And Isaiah called this day "the day of the LORD of hosts" [5], for it is the day of His chastening of His people.

22.3.0.en: 8 And he discovered the covering of Judah, and thou didst look in that day to the armour of the house of the forest. 9 Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many: and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool. 10 And ye have numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and the houses have ye broken down to fortify the wall. 11 Ye made also a ditch between the two walls for the water of the old pool: but ye have not looked unto the maker thereof, neither had respect unto him that fashioned it long ago.

22.3.1.en: What was Judah's attitude to what had happened to Jerusalem? They ignored "the covering of the Most High," which protects and fortifies them, as the psalmist says: "He that dwelleth in the covering of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the God of heaven" (Ps 91:1), "I will trust in the covering of thy wings" (Ps 61:4). By this grace forsook them and they were exposed before the enemy in weakness. "And he discovered the covering of Judah, and thou didst look in that day to the armour of the house of the forest" [8].

22.3.2.en: Some see that the "covering" here refers to the veil that noble women used to wear to hide their faces. For the prophet looked at Judah as a spiritual bride of God who rejected her Bridegroom and lost her purity and chastity and removed her veil shamelessly, desired by strangers, and gives her body to them. This picture applies to Judah when the walls began to be torn down and Jerusalem became like an uncovered face for which strangers lust.

22.3.3.en: Judah tried to find a solution to the problem, but instead of returning to God, it used purely human calculations to achieve deliverance; among them:

22.3.4.en: A. The people rushed to "the house of the forest," which wise Solomon built (1 Kgs 7:2 etc.), in which he placed golden weapons, which Shishak king of Egypt stole, and Rehoboam replaced them with weapons of bronze. The house was full of weapons, but they could not support the people and protect them against the enemies.

22.3.5.en: B. Concern for the waters of the lower pool and turning the waters from outside the walls into the city, so that the enemies outside the walls would not benefit from them and the besieged people would not be exposed to thirst and lack of water.

22.3.6.en: C. The walls began to crack, so they thought of tearing down their houses and turning the rubble toward the wall to protect it from collapse. They did not think of God, the true wall, which the enemy cannot approach; God, who sets up His grace to guard our inner walls so that they are not torn down, for it is said: "By my God have I leaped over a wall" (Ps 18:29), "Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me" (Isa 49:16).

22.4.0.en: 12 And in that day did the Lord GOD of hosts call to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth: 13 And behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen, and killing sheep, eating flesh, and drinking wine: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die. 14 And it was revealed in mine ears by the LORD of hosts, Surely this iniquity shall not be purged from you till ye die, saith the Lord GOD of hosts.

22.4.1.en: God in His love for us calls us to repentance, that we may weep and mourn over our sins, and so enjoy a surpassing inner peace and an unceasing eternal joy; but man in his short-sightedness wants to enjoy temporary pleasure and worldly luxury, reckoning that he will die tomorrow.

22.4.2.en: "And in that day did the Lord GOD of hosts call to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth: and behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen, and killing sheep, eating flesh, and drinking wine: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die" [12-13].

22.4.3.en: * These wicked ones head toward killing themselves with every kind of lust... Yes, for even when they live they are in shame, since they count their belly their god, and when they die they are tormented.

22.5.0.en: 15 Thus saith the Lord GOD of hosts, Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house, and say, 16 What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, as he that heweth him out a sepulchre on high, and that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock? 17 Behold, the LORD will carry thee away with a mighty captivity, and will surely cover thee. 18 He will surely violently turn and toss thee like a ball into a large country: there shalt thou die, and there the chariots of thy glory shall be the shame of thy lord's house. 19 And I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down.

22.5.1.en: Opinions differ concerning Shebna's position in the palace of King Hezekiah; here he appears to be in charge of the king's treasury, and in (2 Kgs 18:37) he is called the scribe, and some see that he was a counsellor to the king or the chief chamberlain of the palace or a minister... In any case he had great authority. And it appears that he was of foreign race. He wanted to immortalize his memory, so he hewed out for himself a great tomb in the very rock in which the kings of Judah were buried. He was a wicked man, so Isaiah rebuked him and called him "the shame of the king's house," and prophesied his removal and the setting up of Eliakim in his place, and this was fulfilled around the year 701 BC.

22.5.2.en: His evil is poured out first in his not believing the words of the prophet Isaiah to the people that they would be taken captive, and his hewing of the tomb was a sign of his unbelief in the prophecies of Isaiah. The other side of the evil is his love of grandeur, for he wanted to be buried with the kings; and finally he was not faithful to the king, for he abused the king's trust in him. For all this the divine judgment was issued to remove him and deprive him of burial in what his hands had built, and instead of his enjoying splendid chariots, he is thrown into a strange city like a ball that a child throws and plays with unhindered.

22.5.3.en: Many see that Shebna is a symbol of the Antichrist who appears in the last days, or of the man of sin who in his pride wishes not to be buried in the tomb of the kings of Judah, the offspring of David, but to sit enthroned in the temple of the Lord and set himself forth as God (2 Thess 2:4). As for Eliakim, he points to the Lord Christ, who shatters the Antichrist and strips him of his might in order to save the elect.

22.6.0.en: It is noticed here that the prophet did not say of Shebna that King Hezekiah would remove him. Rather he says: "Behold, the LORD will carry thee away with a mighty captivity, and will surely cover thee. He will surely violently turn and toss thee (that is, hurl thee with a strong thrust) like a ball into a large country... And I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down" [17-19].

22.7.s.en: 5. The setting up of Eliakim in place of Shebna:

22.7.0.en: 20 And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah: 21 And I will clothe him with thy robe, and strengthen him with thy girdle, and I will commit thy government into his hand: and he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah. 22 And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open. 23 And I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place; and he shall be for a glorious throne to his father's house. 24 And they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, the offspring and the issue, all vessels of small quantity, from the vessels of cups, even to all the vessels of flagons. 25 In that day, saith the LORD of hosts, shall the nail that is fastened in the sure place be removed, and be cut down, and fall; and the burden that was upon it shall be cut off: for the LORD hath spoken it.

22.7.1.en: The speech here [20-25] opens the door of hope before every soul that the enemy of good tries to shatter, for Shebna must necessarily pass away and come to an end and Eliakim take his place. The Antichrist or the false prophet or the man of sin will bear authority and power, but he will certainly collapse, that the Kingdom of Christ may be declared forever.

22.7.2.en: The prophecy came clearly here that Eliakim is a symbol of the Lord Christ.

22.8.0.en: A. "And I will clothe him with thy robe, and strengthen him with thy girdle, and I will commit thy government into his hand: and he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah" [21].

22.8.1.en: Shebna prided himself on the robe and the girdle along with the authority, commanding and forbidding as the second man, the one the king trusted, acting in a spirit of power and arrogance. But when Eliakim takes his place he takes his robe and girdle, yet he bears a spirit of tender fatherhood toward the people of God. The "Antichrist" has authority with violence and harshness, while "Christ" is love and tenderness and surpassing spiritual fatherhood. What distinguishes the children of God from the children of the devil is love full of tenderness as opposed to authority full of violence.

22.8.2.en: It was said of the Lord Christ: "The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty; the LORD is clothed with strength, wherewith he hath girded himself" (Ps 93:1). And the prophet Isaiah saw Him clothed in garments red like him that treadeth in the winefat (Isa 63:1-3). For He clothed Himself with His Church, which He dyed with His precious blood, so that it was sanctified and bore His splendor.

22.8.3.en: He girded Himself to wash the feet and to serve in a spirit of love and humility.

22.9.0.en: B. "And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open" [22]. Who has the key but "he that is holy, he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth" (Rev 3:7). It is the Lord Christ, who encourages His Church, saying to her that He alone opens to her the doors of heaven and shuts her in, so that the devil and all his powers cannot approach her. As for the key with which He opens and shuts, it is: "the authority of binding and loosing" which the Lord gave to His Bride through His disciples (Mt 16:19), as St. Cyril the Great and St. Jerome say; and the Cross, by which our Lord Jesus opens His paradise and with it shuts the gates of hell against us, as St. John Chrysostom says; and also the understanding of the Holy Bible, especially the prophecies that were formerly sealed and not understood, as St. Gregory the Wonderworker says. Origen also says: [Every written work needs the Logos who shut it, in order to open it, "he shutteth, and no man openeth," and when He opens, no one can cast doubt on the explanation He gives].

22.9.1.en: We do not wonder at the saying "And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder," for this key is the Cross which the Son of David carried upon His shoulder to accomplish our salvation.

22.10.0.en: C. "And I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place; and he shall be for a glorious throne to his father's house. And they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, the offspring and the issue, all vessels of small quantity, from the vessels of cups, even to all the vessels of flagons" [23-24].

22.10.1.en: In poor rural areas a person finds no place in his house for many of his needs and possessions, so he hangs them on nails in the wall: clothes, kitchen utensils, laundry, etc... Now the prophet sees that the Messiah, the Savior, is this nail or peg fastened in a sure place, on which the believer hangs all his possessions and needs, and this in the Church, "his father's house." This is a symbolic picture meaning the believer's reliance on the Lord Christ, who dwells in His Church and bears all our burdens. Upon Him faithful kings place the crowns of their kingdom, and upon Him the poor man places his simple needs. He is the support of the great and the poor without distinction.

22.10.2.en: Every vessel - whatever its value - that is hung upon Him becomes a vessel of honor. So the believer says with the Apostle Paul: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us" (2 Cor 4:7).

22.11.0.en: This is about faith in the Lord Christ, the firm nail in the Church, the house of the Father; so what is meant by the removal of the nail [25]?

22.11.1.en: Some see that this removal means the Jews' rejection of the crucified Christ, so that those who have the prophecies concerning Him, and the types with them, pass away from their midst and are shattered. And some see that it points here to what the Jews at that time reckoned a sure, firm nail (Shebna or another), comparing faith in the Messiah, the Savior, with reliance on human ways of salvation.
